claims.statement: The page declares FPT, GHEC and GHES versions, but protected-branch availability is plan/visibility constrained: public Free user/organization repositories and public/private Pro, Team, Enterprise Cloud or Enterprise Server repositories. Redirects and category metadata are navigation, not policy adoption.
Required status-check job names should be unique across workflows; reused names can produce ambiguous results that block merging.
A configured branch protection rule can enforce requirements on pushes, including pull-request merges, before a collaborator changes a branch.
Only organization-owned repositories can add actors to branch-protection bypass lists.
Branch protection disables force pushes by default for matching branches, but administrators can configure exceptions.
Branch protection prevents deletion by default for matching branches, but the restriction is configurable.
By default, repository administrators and custom roles with bypass-branch-protections permission are exempt; an optional setting applies restrictions to them.
Classic protection can target one branch, all branches, or fnmatch patterns; the release wildcard example is illustrative, not a locally selected branch scope.
Auto-merge can be configured to occur once all merge requirements are met; this is a documented capability, not observed automatic integration.

Only one classic branch protection rule applies at a time, unlike cumulative rulesets. Cross-repository organization rules are conditional on repo-rules-enterprise (GHEC or GHES>3.10); conversion guidance is gated to FPT/GHEC or GHES>=3.23.
The twelve linked settings are configurable capabilities, not a mandate to enable every option; the linked how-to is in this batch, but other destination pages are not certified.

Repository administrators or edit-repository-rules roles can require a chosen approval count; when required reviews are enabled, changes go through an approved pull request with write-permission reviewers or a designated owner.
An administrator who requests changes must later approve for merge; if a blocking reviewer is unavailable, a write-permission collaborator can dismiss that review.
Other open pull requests sharing the same head commit can block a reviewed pull request when their reviews are pending or rejected; a writer must approve or dismiss the blocking review.
Attempting to merge with pending or rejected required reviews produces an error; the shown GH006 transcript is illustrative, not an observed negative test.
Optional stale-approval dismissal tracks the approved diff, including changes caused by new commits, Update branch or related merges; a changed diff requires fresh approval.
Review dismissal can optionally be restricted to designated people or teams.
Optional code-owner review requires approval by an owner of affected owned code; this is distinct from ordinary approval count.

An optional latest-reviewable-push approval must come from someone other than its pusher; earlier reviews remain unless stale dismissal is enabled, and an existing reviewer may reapprove. The source recommends stale dismissal against hijacked approved changes.

With stale dismissal or latest-push approval enabled, a directly pushed manually made merge must exactly match GitHub’s generated merge; a merge-base change introducing new content also invalidates approvals.
Required status checks may conclude successful, skipped or neutral and may be checks or commit statuses; a configured gate is not proof that its analysis actually ran.

External services can set commit statuses. Any person or integration with repository write permission can set them, but an expected recently reporting GitHub App can be selected; other publishers then block merge. With any-source mode the source says status authors can still be inspected manually.
After required status checks pass, changes can be pushed to another branch for merge or directly to the protected branch; checks alone do not require a pull request.

Strict checks require an up-to-date base and are the documented default, with extra builds; loose checks omit that requirement and risk post-merge incompatibility; disabled check requirements permit merges irrespective of CI freshness.
Optional conversation resolution requires pull-request comments to be addressed or acknowledged before protected-branch merge.
Required signing allows only signed, verified commits; the source explicitly includes bots on FPT/GHEC and does not make signing a universal obligation.

On FPT/GHEC vigilant-mode partially verified commits are permitted under required signing; an unsigned push requires rewriting with a verified signature and force-pushing, subject to the other protections.

The signed-commit reusable allows signed local commits. On FPT/GHEC a test merge checks introduced head commits, so unsigned head commits can block even a signed squash result; remediation is rewrite/sign or authorized bypass. On GHES the reusable says web pull-request merging is unavailable in this context.
Locally merged commits must be signed before push; a separate pull-request requirement can require bypass permission for that local push. Source signing and pull-request rules must be composed.
Linear history rejects merge commits and requires squash or rebase integration; the repository must allow one of those merge methods before enabling the requirement.

Merge queue evaluates required checks against the latest target plus preceding queued pull requests; a writer can enqueue after existing protections pass, using Actions or another CI provider. Queue merging uses the configured strategy.
A branch rule can require successful deployment to chosen environments before merge; staging is an example rather than an adopted production or environment policy.
Locking makes a branch read-only and undeletable; fork syncing is disabled by default, with an option to allow upstream pulls while preventing other contributions.
The no-bypass setting extends restrictions to administrators and bypass-branch-protections roles, which otherwise have a default exemption.

FPT/GHEC push restrictions are available for Free organization public repositories and Team/Enterprise Cloud organization repositories; authorized users, teams and apps still must satisfy required status checks and pull-request rules.

Matching-branch creation can be restricted too. Grants require repository write access for users, teams or installed apps; the source says administrators and admin apps can always push/create in this push-access setting, to be composed with the separately documented no-bypass option.
Force-push exceptions may admit all repository writers including admins, or only selected people/teams; the default block is not evidence that exceptions are absent.
Force pushes can remove collaborators’ history, corrupt pull requests or introduce unapproved commits; enabling them does not bypass other rules such as linear history.
On GHES a site-wide force-push ban prevents branch exceptions; a default-branch-only ban still permits enabling force pushes on other protected branches.
Allow-deletion admits any repository writer, but a locked branch remains undeletable even for otherwise authorized actors.

scope: Primary reading of full pinned article and recursively included dependencies. Reviewed source statements only; no adoption or live platform verification.
